title: Reported r_t does fall in every re-scored run; 'no downward trend' contradicts the saved data
quote: at 10−5), with no downward trend; as a share of re-scored pass@1 it is 17% at
explanation: Recomputing r_t from the saved re-score files (experiments/viec3/review_cpu/patched/*.json) gives 18.3→16.8→15.7% (Run A, 5×10⁻⁴, seed 1), 18.1→17.6→15.5% (seed 2) and 18.3→17.8→17.5→16.8→16.8% (10⁻⁵, seed 0): a monotone decline of 1.5–2.8 points in all three runs, never rising between rounds; a problem-level bootstrap of the change gives about [−5.3, +0.3], [−5.2, +0.1] and [−2.9, −0.1], so the 10⁻⁵ interval excludes zero. The paper's range 15.5–18.4% is exactly these endpoints, but the text says 'with no downward trend'. The seed-2 pass@1-based share computed from App B also falls (17.6%→14.7%) and is not reported. Under the paper's own logic ('If the model learns to write what V accepts, r_t should fall') this is the predicted adaptation signature, so the headline conclusion is not merely overstated but, as reported, contradicted. Whether the fall is adaptation or an artefact (see the next two issues) must be resolved before any conclusion is drawn; either way the text must report the trend and an interval.

title: The gold-storage defect is fixed by the problem, so r_t cannot test writing adaptation as constructed
quote: the bare gold is parsed to its first number and no longer
explanation: App B says the bare gold is parsed to its first number, so a correct boxed prediction cannot match it. The failure is therefore determined by how the gold is stored, not by how the model writes: on the ~50–60 defect-eligible problems, 94–98% of V′-accepted generations are rejected by V in every round (recomputed from the saved re-scores), and almost the only V-accepts there are unboxed. The only ways the model could 'avoid' the defect are to drop \boxed on those problems or to write an answer that matches the mis-parsed gold. Moreover V′ wraps the gold only when the prediction contains \boxed, so unboxed predictions enter only the denominator: the falling \boxed share (52%→36%) lowers r_t mechanically, and r_t restricted to boxed predictions is flat (~20%). The 15.5–18.4% also includes golds that were wholly unparseable (46 of 51 become parseable once wrapped), a component no adaptation can reduce. Train-on-gold, with no verifier in the loop, moves the share with style alone. Net: r_t as instantiated conflates problem mix, unboxing drift and unparseable golds; a flat or falling r_t is uninterpretable without (a) showing that a V-accepted correct form exists on the affected problems, (b) separating the unparseable-gold component, and (c) handling unboxed predictions symmetrically.

title: The direction-free test has no demonstrated sensitivity: no interval, no positive control, weak SFT pressure
quote: it rules out strong adaptation to this defect, not weak adaptation or adaptation
explanation: The claim that the test 'rules out strong adaptation' is never quantified. r_t has no interval or trend test, comes from three runs (two trained checkpoints each at 5×10⁻⁴), and one of the three runs is at 10⁻⁵, where the paper itself says the adapter barely changes outputs — the same reason it dismisses the patch control as uninformative. In offline rejection-sampling SFT the only pressure against a rejected form is that ~18% of correct samples are left out of the pool; there is no negative gradient, so even a model that 'learns the verifier' may barely move r_t. There is no positive control (e.g. a synthetic defect on a frequent, avoidable format) showing what change in r_t adaptation would produce, and no stated threshold for 'strong'. Contrast with Egashira et al., who observe in RLVR that models unlearn behaviour triggering format-based false negatives — evidence that the effect exists under RL pressure, and a natural calibration target.

title: 'The model does not adapt to this defect' is stated categorically in the abstract, intro and conclusion
quote: the model does not adapt to this defect
explanation: The abstract ('the model does not adapt to this defect'), introduction ('the model does not learn to avoid it') and conclusion state a flat negative, while §5.3 concedes only that the evidence 'rules out strong adaptation to this defect, not weak adaptation or adaptation to others', with no interval on r_t. Given that r_t actually declines in all three re-scored runs, that the defect is largely unavoidable by writing, and that sensitivity is not shown (issues above), the categorical wording is not supported. The paper applies a strict standard elsewhere (App C: a single interval that excludes zero is not sufficient evidence) but not to its own post hoc headline test.

title: Novelty overstated: Egashira et al. and TinyV already track verifier false negatives on the policy's own rollouts over training
quote: TinyV and Huang et al. measure false-reject rates to repair or compare verifiers, and Egashira et al. inject hand-designed error patterns
explanation: The paper's central novelty claim is that none of the surveyed studies 'uses the verifier's false-reject rate on the loop's own outputs, round by round, as a test of whether the model adapts to the verifier'. Egashira et al. (arXiv:2605.02909) estimate FPR and FNR from the policy's own 256 rollouts at every training step (§3, §4.1, Fig. 2) and report for a format-based false-negative pattern that 'the model first unlearns behavior that triggers false negatives' (§4.2) — i.e. the very adaptation the proposed test is meant to detect, already measured in RLVR. TinyV (arXiv:2505.14625, §4.1, Figs. 3–4) tracks rule-verifier false negatives across GRPO steps (≈20% of rollouts per step; the share of prompts with an FN rises to ~47–50%). App A describes these works only as injecting hand-designed patterns and as measuring false-reject rates 'to repair or compare verifiers'. The contribution must be repositioned (e.g. applying such tracking to offline SFT, or as an audit protocol), and the 'applies to RLVR' argument loses its novelty.

title: 'Nor does it improve' / 'negative on the first branch' turn a non-detection into evidence of absence, with no power analysis
quote: Our answer is negative on the first branch.
explanation: The body correctly says 'Not detectably', but the abstract ('Nor does it improve.') and intro ('Our answer is negative on the first branch') state an absence. With 150 problems the minimum detectable effect is roughly 9–10 points for pass@1, ~8 for pass@k and ~4–5 for sample accuracy (SE of pass@1 ≈3.8 points per the paper); pass@1/pass@k upper interval ends reach +8.0 and +7.3. The 2.2-point bound is the largest upper end across ~13 runs (low joint coverage), on a post hoc primary measure, without an equivalence margin and without training-seed variance (≈3.2 points from one replicate). The null therefore excludes only gains as large as the RLVR results the paper cites. A pre-specified equivalence margin or a power analysis is needed before 'does not improve' can be claimed.

title: Without a positive reference, the null speaks to this training recipe, not to the GVT loop
quote: On a held-out exam, the first answer is no: on the four measures fixed in advance
explanation: No arm in any design improves on its round 0, including training on reference solutions, which loses ~20 points of pass@4 at 5×10⁻⁴, and the no-filter arm (≈70% wrong solutions) does about as well as the verifier-filtered arm. With nothing showing that this recipe (LoRA r=16 on q/v, loss over the prompt, 512-token training limit that truncates 24–26% of the pool, one epoch, untuned learning rates) can improve a 1.5B model at all, the absence of a gain cannot be attributed to self-training or to the verifier. J.12 acknowledges this, but the abstract, §5.1 and §7 still state the null as a finding about GVT. The higher-rate declines likewise may reflect optimisation fragility rather than self-training (train-on-gold collapses within one adapter, whereas Run A's first adapter is roughly flat).

title: Title and Contribution 1 headline a post hoc, unvalidated test; its power, its learnability condition and its confounds are not shown
quote: A Direction-Free Test of Verifier Adaptation
explanation: The title, the abstract ("We propose a test that separates the two") and Contribution 1 present the r_t test as the paper's main methodological contribution, and say it "separates" mathematics from verifier learning and "applies to RLVR as well as to SFT". §5.3 itself says the four checks "were defined post hoc here; we offer them as a protocol for future studies, not as tested methods", and "We have not run it on RL checkpoints." Nowhere does the paper show the test can detect adaptation. There is no positive control: no run, synthetic or real, in which the model is known to learn a verifier-accepted form and r_t falls. So a flat r_t cannot be told apart from a test with no power. Two validity conditions are also left open. (1) Learnability: r_t can fall only if V accepts some correct form on the problems the defect affects. For the gold-storage defect the bare gold is parsed to its first number (App B), so it is not shown that any correct form V accepts exists for those problems. If none does (as with the 51 unparseable golds, which "never enter the training pool"), the defect cannot be learned and a flat r_t is guaranteed. (2) Separating adaptation from drift: the re-score wraps the gold only "when the prediction contains" \boxed, so any general move away from \boxed lowers r_t mechanically. The test then has the same imitation-versus-drift ambiguity the paper uses to set aside the \boxed measure (§4.4, App G). It is also fragile to accuracy-driven changes in the problem mix, so "direction-free" holds only to a first approximation. Applying it to public RLVR checkpoints needs a known, frequent defect in *their* verifier. The defect used here is a bug in this pipeline's gold storage, not a property of math-verify, so it does not carry over. A title, abstract and contribution list that lead with this test should say plainly, at least in the abstract and Contribution 1, that it is a post hoc proposal with untested sensitivity. The defensible headline is the negative empirical result (no detectable gain, declines at high LR) together with a proposed audit.

title: Related work omits prior results that bear directly on how to read the flat r_t (RL models do adapt to format-based false negatives; FN rates can rise over training)
quote: and find that systematic false negatives behave like random noise whereas false
explanation: App. A cites Egashira et al. only for 'systematic false negatives behave like random noise' and says the paper's controls cannot test that finding. It leaves out the result that matters most for the proposed r_t test. In RLVR, Egashira et al. observe the model actively unlearning behaviour that triggers a format-based false negative (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.02909, §4.2), so the FNR falls. TinyV observes the opposite trend under GRPO: false negatives accumulate as the policy explores answer formats the verifier does not parse (https://arxiv.org/html/2505.14625, §4.1). Taken together, prior work shows that the step-wise false-reject rate can fall (adaptation) or rise (format drift) during RL. The paper's flat r_t (15.5–18.4%) is a third pattern. It needs to be set against these and explained. An obvious candidate explanation is the paradigm difference the paper itself names. Rejection-sampling SFT never gives a gradient against rejected samples; it only drops them. So adaptation can happen only if the accepted pool's format distribution shifts and the next fresh adapter imitates that shift. RL with negative advantages pushes probability away from rejected outputs directly. Without this comparison, a reader may take 'the model does not adapt to this defect' as a general property of verifier adaptation rather than a property of this paradigm and dose. This also weakens §1/§5.3's claim that the test 'applies to RLVR as well as to SFT' as a new tool: in RLVR, Egashira et al. have already run it.

title: Composition confound: r_t pools over problems, and its movement is set by which problems are solved
quote: rejects does not fall over rounds, so for this one defect the model does not learn
explanation:
Because flips are nearly all-or-nothing per problem (finding 2), r_t ≈ (V'-accepts on the ~50 defect-eligible problems) / (V'-accepts on all problems). Any change in how accuracy is spread across problems moves r_t, whatever the model learns about V. If training hurts compound-answer (often harder) problems more, r_t falls. If it hurts simple-number problems more, r_t rises. Seed 1 shows this: flips fall 144 → 89 (−38%) while all V'-accepts fall 787 → 566 (−28%), so r_t drops even though the within-problem flip rate on eligible problems is unchanged (96.6% → 93.7%). The train-on-gold runs, which have no verifier in the loop, show r_t moving the other way, 18.2% → 21.5% and 18.0% → 20.2%. Shifts of ±2–3 points thus occur with no verifier pressure at all, the same size as the self-training changes. A valid test should be computed within problem: for example, the per-problem flip rate among V'-accepts on defect-eligible problems that are solved in both rounds, or a problem-fixed-effects estimate. The pooled statistic confounds adaptation with changes in which problems are solved.

Related: r_t is not adjusted for the changing problem mix, although the paper applies matching to finished accuracy for exactly this reason — The gold-storage defect is triggered by how a problem's gold answer is stored, combined with the prediction's form. So whether a V'-accepted generation is rejected by V depends largely on which problems the model solves. As accuracy falls and the solved set changes (Table 4: 14–36 problems lost per run), r_t can stay flat while the per-problem rejected fraction falls, or the reverse. This is a composition effect. For finished accuracy the paper recognises this exact problem ('Because the problems that still finish change') and builds a matched metric. The r_t test, which supports the headline 'no adaptation' claim, gets no such treatment. A within-problem version (restricted to problems whose gold triggers the defect, weighted by a fixed problem mix), with a problem-clustered bootstrap, would apply the paper's own standard. Related point: the falling \boxed share (52%→36%) is a change in prediction form that interacts with a defect described as penalising \boxed answers. The paper should state the direction of that interaction for r_t.

Suggested fix: r_t should be computed within problems or on defect-eligible problems only.

title: Three different figures for the defect's rejection share (15.5–18.4%, "about one in six", 17%/20% of pass@1) rest on different denominators
quote: 20% throughout at 10−5
explanation:
The abstract and §3.2 give 15.5–18.4% of V′-accepted generations over all 500 problems. The introduction and conclusion round this to "about one in six". §5.3 and App B then add that, as a share of re-scored exam pass@1, the defect rejects 17% at seed 1 but "20% throughout at 10−5". That is one in five, outside the 15.5–18.4% band quoted as "every round" of the same runs. The difference comes from denominators: all samples on 500 problems versus first-sample pass@1 on the 150-problem exam. The paper does not say this, and §5.3 puts the two figures side by side as if they measured the same r_t. This matters because r_t's flatness is the main evidence for the "no adaptation" claim. The paper should state which denominator defines r_t, give r_t per round and per run in a table, and explain why the exam share differs.

Related: Different statistics are reported under one name (generation-level r_t vs exam pass@1 share) — The abstract and §3.2 give 15.5–18.4%: generation-level V'-accept shares, pooled over all 500 problems and all k samples. §5.3 and App B also cite 17% (seed 1, round 0 and round 2) and 20% throughout at 1e-5. These are (V' pass@1 − V pass@1)/V' pass@1 on the 150-problem exam, first sample only. That is a different denominator, a different subset of problems, and about 40–60 correct answers per round. Read together, '17% at round 0 and round 2' looks like a flat statistic, while the generation-level r_t for the same run falls 18.3% → 15.7%. The exam-share figure is also very noisy: one problem on a 150-problem exam is 0.67 points of pass@1, so 4.7/28.0 vs 6.7/40.0 can be equal by chance. The 20% at 1e-5 lies outside the 15.5–18.4% range quoted as covering 'every round of the three runs'. The paper should report one pre-specified statistic (the generation-level r_t with intervals) and describe the exam share as a separate descriptive figure, or drop it.

Related: 'Correct solutions' and 'one in six' gloss over the definition of the numerator and denominator — The introduction and abstract describe r_t as 'the share of the model's own correct solutions that a known verifier defect rejects'. In fact the denominator is V'-accepted generations (finding 7), and V' differs from V only for boxed predictions (finding 3). An unboxed correct answer that V wrongly rejects can never appear in the numerator. For eligible problems the denominator mixes ~50 problems where the share is ~96% with ~230–280 where it is 0%. 'About one in six' is thus not a per-solution rejection probability. It is a mixture weight set by how many compound-gold problems the model solves. Readers will take it as a uniform false-negative rate and will expect 'adaptation' to show up as a smooth decline of that rate. The paper should present the statistic as a problem-mixture quantity and report the within-eligible flip rate (~96%) alongside it.

Related: Two different r_t-like statistics are reported for the same test, and the 10^-5 value (20%) falls outside the headline range — The abstract and §5.3 give r_t as 15.5–18.4% 'in every round' of three runs, including 10^-5. The same paragraph then gives a second figure, the defect's share of re-scored exam pass@1: 17% at seed 1 and '20% throughout at 10−5'. App B shows the 15.5–18.4% is computed over all 500 problems and all generations, while the 17%/20% is computed on the exam set's pass@1. The two have different denominators and different noise levels; pass@1 is a single draw on 150 problems. A reader cannot tell which is the test statistic, and 20% at 10^-5 sits outside the 15.5–18.4% band that the abstract says holds in every round of every run. The paper should define one statistic and report it per run and round, with an interval.

title: 'No false accepts by V'' is assumed, yet the paper's own hand check found one
quote: one prediction had an empty box
explanation: The test counts every V'-accept as correct ('share of correct solutions'). App B says the 15.5–18.4% figure 'assumes that the re-scored verifier itself accepts no wrong answer, which we did not measure'. But in the 30-flip hand check, one flip was an empty \boxed{} that V' accepted: a V' false accept, about 3% of flips (binomial 95% CI roughly 0.1–17%). Wrapping the gold also changes how compound golds parse (for example, whether 137 \frac{1}{2} is read as a mixed number or as a product). So V' can accept answers that are differently, but not equivalently, written. If V' false accepts are concentrated in some answer styles whose frequency changes over rounds, r_t moves for reasons unrelated to adaptation. The 'correct solutions' wording in the abstract and introduction should become 'V'-accepted solutions'. A hand audit of V' accepts (not only flips) is needed before r_t can be read as a false-reject rate.

title: False-positive rate left unmeasured, though the audit data permit an estimate and the defect itself implies false positives for both V and V′
quote: so it cannot measure the false-positive rate; that the verifier rarely accepts wrong
explanation: The FN audit scored all 176 parseable-gold MATH-500 solutions with a scripted correctness check: 128 correct, 48 not recognised as correct. The verifier's decision on those 48 is available, so at least an upper bound on the false-positive rate can be computed from data already in hand. 'Inspected only rejections' describes a choice of analysis; it does not mean FP is unmeasurable. FP matters for three claims. (a) The defect description implies a structural FP channel in V: if a bare compound gold such as 3\sqrt{13} is parsed to its first number, then a wrong prediction \boxed{3} matches it. The pool can therefore contain wrong 'accepted' answers on exactly the defect problems, and adapting to V there would mean writing such answers, which r_t (defined over V′-accepted generations) cannot see. (b) The 30-flip hand check found one flip with an empty box. That is an apparent false positive of V′ (~3% of flips), against the stated assumption that V′ accepts no wrong answer. (c) 'Correct' in every table means V-accepted, so FP inflates every pass rate. The paper should report the FP estimate from the audit data, check how often V accepts a prediction equal to the first number of a compound gold, and say what the empty-box case implies for V′.

title: Scaling the 2.2-point bound to ~3 points contradicts the paper's own re-scored intervals
quote: 2.2-point bound on gains, which on the re-scored scale is nearer 3 points
explanation:
The paper takes the factor 0.73–0.78 (a ratio of point estimates in three declining runs: −8.3/−10.7 = 0.78, −4.7/−6.0 = 0.78, −2.4/−3.3 = 0.73) and applies it to 'every original-verifier difference and interval', so the 2.2-point upper bound becomes 2.2/0.75 ≈ 2.9. This would only hold if re-scoring multiplied every per-problem difference by one constant. The re-scored intervals the paper reports do not behave that way. Interval widths barely change: Run A 5e-4 seed 1 goes from [−12.3, −4.5] (width 7.8) to [−14.8, −6.7] (8.1); seed 2 from [−8.2, −1.2] (7.0) to [−9.7, −2.2] (7.5); 1e-5 seed 0 from [−4.8, 0.0] (4.8) to [−5.9, −0.7] (5.2). Widths grow by about 4–8%, not by the ~30% that dividing by 0.75 implies. Meanwhile the point estimates move further negative. The 2.2 bound comes from runs with negative point estimates (A at 1e-4, seeds 1 and 3: −1.5 [−5.3, 2.2] and −1.0 [−4.3, 2.2]). Applying the observed pattern (centre ×1.3, half-width ×1.05) to −1.5 [−5.3, 2.2] gives about −2.0 [−5.9, 2.0]: the upper end stays near 2, it does not move to 3. Rescaling an upper endpoint by a ratio of point estimates only makes sense for an interval centred on a positive gain. Neither run that sets the bound was re-scored. The '≈3 points' figure (also in the summary) is unsupported and probably wrong in direction. It should be dropped, or computed by actually re-scoring the runs that set the bound.

Related: Understatement factor 0.73–0.78 does not fit all re-scored runs and does not rescale intervals — The factor is defined as 'the ratios of original to re-scored sample-accuracy changes below'. For the three self-training runs the ratios are −8.3/−10.7=0.78, −4.7/−6.0=0.78 and −2.4/−3.3=0.73, so 0.73–0.78 is right for them. The same paragraph also gives the train-on-gold changes (−19.7 vs −24.7 and −18.7 vs −22.0, repeated in App G), and those ratios are 0.80 and 0.85, outside the range. The stronger claim, that 'the same factor shrinks every original-verifier difference and interval, including the 2.2-point bound on gains, which on the re-scored scale is nearer 3 points', does not match the re-scored intervals the paper reports. Interval widths change by ratios of 0.92–0.96, not 0.73–0.78 (A,1: 7.8 vs 8.1; A,2: 7.0 vs 7.5; A 10−5: 4.8 vs 5.2). The upper endpoints shift down rather than scale: [−4.8, 0.0] becomes [−5.9, −0.7], and [−8.2, −1.2] becomes [−9.7, −2.2]. Dividing +2.2 by about 0.75 to get 'nearer 3' therefore has no basis in these data. In addition, the 2.2 endpoint comes from the 10−4 runs (seeds 1 and 3), which were never re-scored.

Related: The 0.73–0.78 'understatement factor' is a composite of two effects, is outside range for train-on-gold, and is extrapolated to every table — Arithmetic check: the three self-training ratios are 0.78, 0.78 and 0.73. Train-on-gold, re-scored in the same analysis, gives −19.7/−24.7 = 0.80 and −18.7/−22.0 = 0.85, both outside the stated range. A constant defect share f ≈ 17–20% of correct answers would predict a factor of 1−f ≈ 0.80–0.83. The lower observed 0.73–0.78 is consistent with a second effect: the always-zero unparseable-gold problems (11–18 per partition, ≈7–12%) add no change under V but do under V′. So the factor depends on how many dead problems a partition has and on accuracy changes on those problems; it is not a property of the verifier. Extending it to 'every original-verifier difference and interval', to runs never re-scored (all of 1e-4 and 2e-4, Run B, no-filter, Run C), to pass@k, and to the claim that all tables are '4.7–8.0 points too low' is unsupported. The 4.7–8.0 offsets are pass@1 on MATH-500 exams from five runs. GSM8K (0% audited FN, numeric golds) and Design P are presumably mostly unaffected, and pass@k offsets were not reported. The paper should state the factor's derivation and range (including train-on-gold), limit it to the re-scored runs, and restrict the 'too low' statement to MATH-500 pass@1.

Related: The 2.2-point 'no gain' bound is on a scale known to be shrunk by about 0.75 and omits seed variance of comparable size; §5.1, §6 and §7 state it without these corrections, and 150 problems give little power on the pre-set measures — The paper credits itself correctly for calling the bound 'loose', but several quantified weaknesses are left out of the main-text answer. (1) Appendix B shows that the original verifier understates every change by a factor of about 0.73–0.78 and says the 2.2-point bound 'on the re-scored scale is nearer 3 points'. §5.1, §6 and the Conclusion still report 2.2, and §6 does not list the understatement. (2) I.1 says training-seed variance is 'of the same size' (a replicate ends 3.2 points away). An interval that included it would be wider, perhaps around 5 points, so the bound is loose by a known order of magnitude, not just in principle. (3) Power. The exam has 150 problems, of which 11–18 per partition have unparseable gold and are always unsolved (App B), so the effective n is about 132–139. pass@1 is a single draw per problem (J.3 mentions this only in passing). The resulting pass@1/pass@k intervals are about ±7 points wide (upper ends +8.0 and +7.3). On the pre-set measures, gains that would count as substantial in the self-improvement literature could not be detected. Exam size and power appear nowhere in the limitations list as a limit on the 'no gain' conclusion. Since 'no gain' is one of the paper's two headline results, the Conclusion should give the corrected bound (about 3 points on the re-scored scale, wider with seed variance) and say plainly that on the pre-set pass@1/pass@k a gain of up to about 7–8 points cannot be excluded.

title: Training-seed variance rests on a single replicate pair at a different rate, and the 'same size' comparison mixes a difference with an SD
quote: which is of the same size (a replicate of Run A at 5 × 10−4, seed 1, ends 3.2
explanation: The only direct estimate of training-seed variance is one replicate pair (Run A, 5×10^-4, seed 1). It gives a difference of 3.2 points, a variance estimate with one degree of freedom whose own uncertainty is very large. A difference between two runs has about sqrt(2) times the SD of a single run, so the implied per-run seed SD is about 2.3. The paper calls the 3.2 'of the same size' as the bootstrap half-widths, which compares a difference with a half-width. Also, the bound being questioned (2.2) comes from the 10^-4 and 10^-5 runs, where training changes outputs much less and seed variance could be smaller or larger; there is no replicate at those rates. The second illustration in App C (A vs B at seed 2, 7.3 points of pass@1) is a single-draw pass@1 contrast between arms that differ in treatment. The paper should say explicitly that seed variance is essentially unestimated at the rates behind the no-gain bound, rather than citing a precise-looking 3.2.

title: §4.1 says selection problems fall as much as the exam; App D's numbers show they sometimes fall less
quote: fall as much as the exam)
explanation:
§4.1 defends Design P's selection-set scoring by saying 'in Design I the selection problems fall as much as the exam'. Appendix D's own comparison is mixed. At 10−5, selection falls less (−1.0 and −1.1 against exam −2.4 and −1.4). Run C at 5×10−4 falls clearly less (−11.3 against −15.4). Run A at 5×10−4 seed 1 is −8.2 against −8.3, and only 10−4 seed 1 (−6.2 vs −1.5) and 5×10−4 seed 2 (−5.3 vs −4.7) fall more. App D's phrase 'as much as or more than ... at the two higher rates' is also loose: there are three higher rates, the examples are drawn from 5×10−4 and 10−4, and −8.2 vs −8.3 is slightly less. The main-text summary should match App D's mixed result. A smaller point: App D's exam values (−1.4, −15.4, −13.0) do not match Table 5 (A,1 −1.5; C,1 −15.3; C,0 −13.1). The differences are only rounding, but the paper should use one source.

Related: §4.1 overstates the selection-vs-exam check; at Design P's own learning rate the selection problems fell less, and the differences are within noise — The main text says that in Design I the selection problems 'fall as much as the exam'. Appendix D does not support that as a blanket statement. Selection falls as much or more only at the two higher rates (5e-4: -8.2/-5.3 vs -8.3/-4.7; 1e-4 seed 1: -6.2 vs -1.5). At 1e-5 Run A's selection problems fall less (-1.0 and -1.1 against -2.4 and -1.4/-1.5), less than half the exam decline at seed 0. Run C at 5e-4 also falls less (-11.3 vs -15.4). The rate that matters here is 1e-5, because Design P was trained at 1e-5. At that rate, and for Run A, the comparison leans the other way: training on a problem's own accepted solutions may have partly protected it. Second, Appendix D gives no intervals for these selection-minus-exam differences. With 150 exam problems the sample-accuracy changes alone have intervals about ±2.5–4 points wide (Table 5), so gaps of 1–2 points (and even the 4.7-point gap at 1e-4 seed 1, which has no interval) cannot tell 'falls more', 'as much' and 'less' apart. The honest summary is 'no detectable difference, with a hint of protection at 1e-5'. That supports 'unlikely to have masked' only weakly. It does not support App D's further remark that selection scoring 'may have enlarged' the decline, which rests on noise-level gaps at other rates. The main text should match the appendix: mixed results, slightly less decline at 1e-5, no intervals.

title: Exam declines quoted in App D's selection-set comparison do not match Table 5
quote: less (−1.0 and −1.1 against −2.4 and −1.4), and Run C’s selection problems
explanation: App D compares selection-set declines with exam declines, but three of the exam figures differ from Table 5's sample-accuracy column. Run A, 1e-5, seed 1 is -1.4 in App D and -1.5 in Table 5. Run C at 5e-4 is -15.4 in App D ('-11.3 against -15.4') and -15.3 in Table 5. Run C at 1e-5 is -13.0 in App D ('-13.8 against -13.0') and -13.1 in Table 5. The differences are probably due to the separate re-scoring mentioned in Appendix C, but App D does not say which scoring it uses, and the same comparison mixes figures that do match Table 5 (-8.3, -4.7, -1.5 at 1e-4) with figures that do not. App D should state the scoring source or use the Table 5 values. These gaps are small, but they are the same size as the selection-minus-exam differences the argument relies on (e.g. -13.8 vs -13.0 is reported as 'slightly more').

title: A seed-0 sample-accuracy interval with upper end 0.0 is described as excluding zero
quote: exclude zero (upper ends −0.6 and 0.0 for sample accuracy, −0.5 and −0.9
explanation:
In Table 5, the 10−5 sample-accuracy interval for A, seed 0 is −2.4 [−4.8, 0.0]. An interval that ends at 0.0 does not exclude zero. Appendix E contradicts itself here. It first says sample accuracy falls 'with one interval (B, seed 0) excluding zero', then says 'These seed-0 intervals only just exclude zero (upper ends −0.6 and 0.0 for sample accuracy ...)', which counts A's [−4.8, 0.0] as excluding zero. §4.2 likewise says 'sample accuracy falls 1.2–3.2 points and matched finished accuracy 1.1–4.2, with intervals that only just exclude zero for A and B at seed 0', which a reader will take to cover both measures. Only the matched intervals (upper ends −0.5 and −0.9) and B's sample-accuracy interval (−0.6) actually exclude zero. App G handles the same situation correctly, saying two pass@4 intervals 'reach zero at their upper end'.

Related: Sample-accuracy interval for A, seed 0 does not exclude zero, yet §4.2 and App E say it does — §4.2 says the sample-accuracy and matched finished-accuracy intervals 'only just exclude zero for A and B at seed 0'. In Table 5 the sample-accuracy interval for A, seed 0 is [-4.8, 0.0]. Its upper end is 0.0, so it includes zero, or at best touches it. Only B, seed 0 ([-5.9, -0.6]) excludes zero. Appendix E first says this correctly ('one interval (B, seed 0) excluding zero'). A few lines later it says 'These seed-0 intervals only just exclude zero (upper ends -0.6 and 0.0 for sample accuracy ...)', which contradicts itself because an upper end of 0.0 does not exclude zero. Both lists of upper ends also switch order: -0.6 and 0.0 is B then A, while -0.5 and -0.9 matched is A then B. The right count is: for sample accuracy, 1 of 4 MATH-500 intervals excludes zero at 1e-5; for matched finished accuracy, 2 of 4 do, both at seed 0, and the paper itself calls those two close to one replicate. The main text should say this and not merge the two metrics. The conclusion ('possible small decline, not an established one') survives, but the evidence is weaker than §4.2 suggests.

title: Seed-1 ranges for the cap-share and finished-share leave out two seed-1 runs that contradict them
quote: 62–74%, every seed-2 run 34–59%)
explanation:
Appendix H says the finished-accuracy shares 'split by seed (every seed-1 run 62–74%, every seed-2 run 34–59%)', and §4.5, §5.3(ii), the Conclusion and App I.1 say the cap-share part is '12–30% of the decline at seed 1 and 52–72% at seed 2'. I recomputed these from Table 7. A,1 / B,1 / No filter,1 give finished shares of 73/62/74% and cap-share fractions of 1.3/8.3=16%, 2.0/6.7=30% and 1.0/8.2=12%, which matches the stated ranges. Seed 2 also checks out (72%, 52%, 60%). But Table 7 lists two more seed-1 runs at 5×10−4: 'A replicate, 1' (Fin. share 89%, cap-share +0.1 of −5.2, i.e. about −2%) and 'A, 1024 limit, 1' (85%, cap-share −0.3 of −5.7, i.e. about 5%). Both fall outside the stated ranges. So 'every seed-1 run 62–74%' is wrong as written. The 12–30% figure holds only for the three original-configuration seed-1 runs and should say so. This matters because the text reads the split by seed as 'partition variation'. The two extra seed-1 runs show that same-partition runs also reach 85–89%, which weakens that reading and widens the seed-1 cap-share range to about −2% to 30%.

Related: Seed-1 ranges in the anatomy omit the two other seed-1 runs at 5×10⁻⁴ — From Table 7, the cap-share/Δacc at seed 1 is A 1.3/8.3=16%, B 2.0/6.7=30%, no-filter 1.0/8.2=12% (hence 12–30%), and at seed 2 3.4/4.7=72%, 4.8/9.2=52%, 6.1/10.2=60% (52–72%). Both match. But Table 7 also lists two more seed-1 5×10⁻⁴ runs, the replicate (cap-share +0.1/−5.2 ≈ −2%) and the 1024-limit run (0.3/5.7 ≈ 5%), and these fall outside '12–30%'. Likewise the next sentence says 'every seed-1 run 62–74%' for the finished share, while the replicate is 89% and the 1024-limit run 85%. Including them strengthens the seed split rather than weakening it, but 'every seed-1 run' is literally false as written. The ranges should cover all seed-1 rows or state that they cover the A/B/no-filter runs only.

title: "Finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate" drops the matched-metric caveats and mixes run types
quote: 5–11 points less accurate
explanation:
The abstract states as fact, without marking it post hoc, that at the highest rate finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate. Contribution 4 says "finished generations lose 5.5–10.6 points against the untrained model on the same problems". The evidence (Table 5 "Finished, matched", Table 11, App H) carries caveats that neither statement keeps. (a) The metric is post hoc and "conditions on an outcome of training and is descriptive, not a causal effect" (App H). (b) It is not "on the same problems": 22–45 of the 150 problems with no finished last-round sample drop out, the rest are reweighted, and for 6–21 problems the baseline is replaced by all-sample accuracy, which biases it. (c) The 5.5–10.6 range covers six runs, including the two no-filter runs. Those have no verifier in the loop and 3–4× the optimizer steps, and the top value (−10.6) is no-filter seed 1. Verifier-filtered self-training alone gives 5.5–9.1. The replicate and 1,024-limit runs at the same rate (App H: −5.0, −5.7) are left out. (d) One of the six intervals (A seed 2, [−11.7, 0.1]) includes zero. (e) The abstract places the phrase right after "accuracy falls in every run", which includes GSM8K Run C (−12.1 matched) and train-on-gold (−25.6/−25.9), both outside 5–11. So the scope of "5–11" is unclear. (f) Table 7's "Finished" decomposition part, a different quantity, is only −2.7 to −6.0 at the same rate. Readers may mix the two up, and the abstract does not say which one it reports. Suggested wording: "in a post hoc matched comparison, finished generations of verifier-filtered runs at the highest rate are 5.5–9.1 points less accurate (one of four intervals reaching zero)".

Related: Abstract's '5–11 points' covers only some of the runs that 'every run' refers to — The abstract says 'At the highest rate accuracy falls in every run, and finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate'. The 5–11 range (5.5–10.6 in Table 5) comes from the six MATH-500 verifier-filtered and no-filter runs. Other runs at 5×10−4 fall outside it. Train-on-gold loses 25.6 and 25.9 points of matched finished accuracy, and the GSM8K Run C at 5×10−4 loses 12.1. Read literally, 'every run' at the highest rate includes those three, so the range is too narrow. Saying 'the six MATH-500 self-training and no-filter runs' would fix it. The intro states its scope correctly ('what training at the highest rate changes ... 5.5–10.6'), but the abstract does not.

title: Rate dependence and 'cap-hit rises only at 5×10⁻⁴' are weaker than stated, and partly contradicted by the replicate and Table 12
quote: at seed 1 sample accuracy falls 1.5, 3.5 and 8.3 points
explanation:
The values are correct (Table 5: −1.5, −3.5, −8.3 at seed 1; −3.7, −3.8, −4.7 at seed 2), and the appendix hedges ('suggestive, not established'). But the main text's 'may grow with the rate on one seed' leans on the −8.3 endpoint, and the same-configuration replicate at seed 1 and 5×10⁻⁴ gives −5.2 (Table 7). The −8.3 run is therefore an extreme of two draws differing by 3.1 points, the paper's only replicate-noise estimate. That spread exceeds the 2-point gap between 1e-4 and 2e-4 at seed 1. Table 12 is also hard to square with a rate trend. Re-scored on the same seed-1 exam, the 2×10⁻⁴ adapter's deficit to the untrained model (−7.8 at 512 tokens) is as large as the two 5×10⁻⁴ adapters' (−8.0, −8.8), and its proxy-degenerate share (28.7%) is similar to theirs (30.0%, 37.2%). Likewise, §4.4's 'The cap-hit share rises only at 5×10⁻⁴' is true only at seed 2: at seed 1 the 5×10⁻⁴ rises (+3.0 [−1.7, 7.7], +2.3, replicate −0.2, 1024-limit +0.7) are within noise, as Appendix H itself notes. The main text should say the rate dependence is not supported beyond noise at either seed, and that the cap-hit rise is a seed-2 phenomenon.

Related: Introduction and Contribution 4 present the cap-hit rise without the conclusion's "clearly only at one seed" caveat — The introduction says what appears at the highest rate is lower finished accuracy "and more generations that run out of tokens". Contribution 4 says "the cap-hit share rises only at that rate". Both read as a finding that holds across runs at 5×10−4. App H and Table 7 show otherwise: at seed 1 the rise in A (+3.0 [−1.7, 7.7]) and no-filter (+2.3 [−2.5, 6.8]) has an interval including zero, "about the size of two samplings of the untrained model", and the replicate (−0.2) and the 1,024-limit run (+0.7) "do not rise at all". Termination contributes "clearly only at one seed", and the cap-share part ranges from 12–30% to 52–72% depending on seed/partition. The conclusion and App H state this correctly. The introduction and Contribution 4 should carry the same caveat (e.g. "rises clearly only at the highest rate and at one of two seeds"). Otherwise the front matter suggests a robust termination effect that the evidence does not support.

title: The main text presents redundant measures as extra evidence: added/lost counts restate pass@k, and the 'four pre-set measures' include non-gain measures
quote: 500 run but one, the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained.
explanation:
§5.1 lists 'the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained' as a separate supporting fact. §3.4 and I.1 both note that added minus lost equals 150×∆pass@k, so this 'restates the sign of the pass@k change rather than adding evidence'. That caveat appears in the appendix but not in the main-text answer, where the sentence reads as corroboration. Likewise, the Conclusion says 'on the four measures fixed in advance no run improves detectably'. Of the four pre-set measures (pass@1, pass@k, style counts, added/lost; §3.4), style is not a gain measure and added/lost duplicates pass@k, so the null actually rests on two measures: pass@1, a single draw, and pass@k. Presenting four suggests a broader and more independent null than the data give. This is a case where a main-text summary of an appendix drops a qualifier that changes how strong the evidence looks. Suggested fix: add the 'restates pass@k' caveat to §5.1 (or drop the sentence), and in §7 name the gain measures (pass@1 and pass@k) rather than 'the four measures'.

Related: Added/lost counts appear as supporting evidence in §5.1, although §3.4 says they are not an independent test — §3.4 notes that added minus lost equals 150×Δpass@k, 'so these counts add only the gross churn behind the net change, not an independent test'. I.1 likewise says the count 'restates the sign of the pass@k change rather than adding evidence'. The main-text answer in §5.1 drops this qualifier and places the sentence right after the 2.2-point bound, as a further reason for 'Not detectably'. A reader of the main text alone would take it as extra evidence. It is the sign of Δpass@k, which Table 5 already reports with intervals, mostly including zero. The I.1 qualifier should be added to §5.1, or the sentence removed.

Related: "On the four measures fixed in advance no run improves detectably": two of the four measures have no notion of improvement or no interval — The four pre-set measures (§1) are pass@1, pass@k, \boxed style share, and per-problem transitions. Only pass@1 and pass@k have bootstrap intervals (Table 5), so "detectably" is defined only for them. Style is not a measure of mathematical improvement at all. Transitions are reported as raw added/lost counts with no interval, and §5.1 states that "In every MATH-500 run but one, the problems lost equal or outnumber those gained". For example, Run A seed 3 at 10−4 has 16 added / 14 lost (Table 4), a net gain on that measure. The conclusion's sentence extends a claim established for two measures to all four. It should say "neither pass@1 nor pass@k improves detectably in any run, and transitions are net-negative in all but one MATH-500 run".

title: Abstract calls both controls "underpowered"; the no-filter control is dose-confounded, not underpowered, and shows a directional result
quote: that patch a rarer defect or remove the filter are underpowered and show
explanation: "Underpowered" fits the \dfrac patch, whose treatment changes 0–4 training examples (§4.3, App F). It does not describe the no-filter control. That control changes the training data massively (1,400 unfiltered examples against about 440 filtered, 3–4× the optimizer steps), so its problem is a dose/data confound, not a weak treatment (App G: "dose and data differ at once"). It is also not simply "no consistent difference": removing the filter lowers pass@4 at both seeds (−2.0, −5.3), and one sample-accuracy interval excludes zero in favour of the filter (−5.5 [−9.2, −1.8] at seed 2). The conclusion describes this more accurately ("removing the filter lowers pass@4 at both seeds, within noise; single-seed intervals sometimes exclude zero"). The abstract should say the no-filter control is confounded by dose and weakly favours the filter on pass@4.

title: The verifier conclusions skip what the no-filter arm and the r_t null say about Egashira et al.; 'no consistent difference' undersells a filter that never helps
quote: The defensible statement about the verifier is narrow: removing a format
explanation: §5.2/I.2 settle on 'removing a format defect present in under 1% of generations, or removing the filter entirely, made no consistent difference', and say that whether systematic false negatives are harmless 'as Egashira et al. find for RLVR, our data cannot say'. Two points make this reasoning incomplete. (1) Removing the filter is not a false-negative manipulation. It turns roughly 70% of training examples into false positives (wrong answers), the error type Egashira et al. find can cause plateau or collapse. The no-filter arm is never better than the filtered arm and is worse at seed 2 (sample accuracy −10.2 vs −4.7; pass@4 lower at both seeds). With 3–4× the dose this cannot be attributed causally, but 'no consistent difference' is a flat summary of a one-sided pattern. The fact that training mostly on wrong solutions does about as well as training on verified ones is itself informative: either the filter adds nothing at this dose, or the recipe dominates (see the positive-reference issue). Neither reading is discussed. (2) The r_t result is the paper's one measurement bearing on a systematic false negative, and it is qualitatively in line with Egashira et al.'s finding that systematic FNs act like noise and are not exploited. The Discussion says the data 'cannot say' anything about this while the Abstract claims 'the model does not adapt to this defect'. The paper should either explain why the r_t null does not bear on Egashira's FN finding (e.g., different paradigm, untested avoidability), or note the consistency with suitable hedges. It should also discuss the no-filter result as a false-positive manipulation.

title: 'Restart-from-base leaves compounding little room' contradicts the data-mediated compounding the paper itself argues for in Design P, and I.2 says the shrinking-pool mechanism has 'no support'
quote: round leaves compounding little room, so the absence of compounding is
explanation: J.7 and §6 present restart-from-base as limiting compounding. That holds only for parameter-level compounding. In the loop as described (§3.1), the round-t pool is generated by the round-(t−1) model, which was itself trained on a pool from the round-(t−2) model, so selection effects can still compound through the data. Appendix D says exactly this: dose 'explains at most the level of the decline, not its time course' (the largest drops come from the smallest pools), and 'Something carried through the data, such as pool composition or style, fits this acceleration better.' That is the self-reinforcing shrinking-pool mechanism, or close to it. Yet I.2 says 'The data give it no support, but they do not rule it out either', and §5.2 says they 'neither support nor rule it out'. The appendix offers some support (accelerating decline with shrinking pools, falling \boxed share, rising $-spans), even if it is not causal evidence, while the Discussion denies any support. Separately, if compounding through data is possible, the 'absence of compounding' in Design I cannot be put down to the restart design. It reflects the short loop (2–4 trained rounds), the small changes at 10^−5, and the lack of a frequent varied defect. Suggested fix: make §5.2/I.2 and App D say the same thing ('weakly consistent with but not tested'), and rewrite J.7 to separate parameter compounding (removed by the design) from data compounding (still possible, and suggested by Design P).

title: Missing or understated limitations: the learning-rate comparison is confounded with k, pool size and number of rounds, and there is only one model family (Qwen2.5), the family where spurious-reward gains are known to appear
quote: The learning-rate grid is coarse, with three
explanation: §6 and J.4 call the higher-rate grid 'coarse' with three rounds and k = 4, but leave out the consequence. Rate is not the only thing that changes across the grid. At 10^−5 the runs use k = 8 and five rounds (round-0 pool 872, about 436 steps). At the higher rates they use k = 4 and three rounds, R0–R2, which is only two trained adapters (pool about 440, about 220 steps), and 'last round' is R4 in one case and R2 in the other (Table 5). So the higher-rate arms have about half the dose and half the training rounds of the 10^−5 arms. The pass@k measure also differs (pass@8 vs pass@4), so ∆pass@k is not comparable across rates. This matters for I.1 and App D, which use 'stronger training produces larger declines' across rates as indirect support for a dose explanation of the Design P collapse: across the grid, rate and dose move in opposite directions. J.7's 'at most five rounds' also hides that most conditions have two trained rounds, which limits any compounding test (see related issue). On scope, §6 says 'one model size in Design I' but not 'one model family'. The paper motivates itself with Shao et al.'s finding that random rewards raise accuracy (§1, §5.3), a result widely reported to depend strongly on Qwen2.5 models. Contamination of MATH-500/GSM8K (J.11) is also a known concern for Qwen2.5 specifically. Whether a sub-2B model 'learns mathematics or the verifier' under GVT may well depend on the family, so this belongs in the scope limitation, next to a note that the across-rate dose-response argument is confounded.

title: Some practical suggestions are unsupported or contradicted by the paper's own evidence, and the most important lessons are left out
quote: 0.5% of the pool cannot be detected with 150 problems
explanation: I.3 rightly says that some suggestions are general good practice, but several are still written as findings. (1) 'A treatment that changes 0.5% of the pool cannot be detected with 150 problems' is a quantitative power claim with no power analysis behind it. The patch null shows non-detection, not undetectability: a small pool change could in principle have a large effect if those examples are influential. (2) 'Check that the training step changes the model (loss and output statistics after one round)' sits awkwardly with J.4, which reports that at 10^−5 'its loss does fall' while outputs barely change. On the paper's own evidence, loss is not a valid check, and only output statistics are. (3) The list leaves out the lessons the paper's evidence supports most directly: run a positive control (or at least a gold-SFT reference that improves) before reading a null (J.12, K); set the training sequence limit to at least the generation cap plus the prompt, since 24–26% of the kept pool is truncated (J.9), which plausibly teaches unfinished outputs; and give an equivalence margin in advance (J.10). (4) 'Hold out evaluation items and keep one adapter per dataset' is offered as a remedy for the Design P artefact, but App D argues selection-set scoring did not hide a decline and may have enlarged one, so the suggestion's basis is ordinary good practice, not the paper's data. Suggested fix: label each suggestion as finding-backed or general practice, and replace the loss check with output statistics.

title: Table 11 gives the same round-0 length for two different exam partitions
explanation: In Table 11, both 10−5 rows (A, seed 0 and A, seed 1) have round-0 mean length 1158 characters (1158 →1147 and 1158 →1146). Seeds 0 and 1 draw different 150-problem exam partitions, and their round-0 cap-hit shares (46.9% vs 40.7%) and finished accuracies (54.8% vs 55.2%) differ. With cap-hit six points apart, an identical mean length to the character is unlikely. Elsewhere, different partitions give different round-0 lengths (1175, 1154, 1178). This may be a transcription error and should be checked.

title: "They do not ask what the gain consists of" is contradicted by the cited RLVR papers themselves
quote: These studies improve accuracy, which our SFT loop does not, but they do not ask what the gain consists of.
explanation: The first cited example is Wang et al.'s 36.0%→73.6% on MATH-500 (verified, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.20571, NeurIPS 2025). Its own abstract decomposes that gain: it reports an '8.6% improvement beyond format correction', which implies most of the jump is format correction. That is the same 'mathematics or format/verifier?' question this paper poses, answered in part by the cited authors. In the sibling cluster, SimpleRL-Zoo (arXiv:2503.18892) analyses response length, reasoning behaviours and format-reward effects across its ten base models. Huang et al. (arXiv:2505.22203), from the same group, studies how rule-based-verifier false negatives shape RL gains. The statement is therefore inaccurate as written. It also hides a useful fact for the paper's motivation: the headline 1.5B RLVR number cited in §1 and §2 is largely a format effect by its authors' own account. That supports the paper's framing better than the current wording, which presents 36.0→73.6 as an unexamined accuracy gain. Suggested change: report the 8.6-point beyond-format figure, and narrow the claim to 'do not test whether the gain reflects adaptation to the verifier's specific defects'.

title: Qiao et al. described as purely theoretical and out of its multi-silo setting
quote: Qiao et al. [8] argue theoretically that a selector seeing only a narrow slice of the target distribution accelerates collapse.
explanation: Qiao et al. (arXiv:2606.13732, ICML 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13732) prove the result and also run experiments. Their setting is siloed selection, where each of several verifiers or institutions sees only a local, biased slice and raw data cannot be pooled, and they propose Wasserstein proxy references as a fix. 'Argue theoretically' undersells the empirical part. Leaving out the multi-silo framing makes the result look more directly applicable to a single rule-based verifier with a format bias than it is. A single format-biased verifier is a different kind of selection bias: it depends on the answer form, not on a local view of the distribution. This is minor, but the main-text paraphrase 'a narrow selector can accelerate collapse' should state the setting.

title: 'The adapter barely changes the outputs' at 1e-5 rests on coarse aggregates and conflicts with the paper's own decline and divergence evidence
quote: on MATH-500 the adapter barely changes the outputs (length and cap-hit share
explanation: This claim carries a lot of weight. It is used to say the flat MATH-500 curve at 1e-5 is uninformative (§4.2), to explain the null patch control (§4.3, App F: 'nearly identical pools would give nearly identical models'), and it motivates the higher-rate runs (§4.4). The only evidence given is that mean length (1158->1147) and cap-hit share (46.9->47.4%, 40.7->41.8%) barely move for Run A. Those are coarse summaries: an adapter can change which answers are produced, the reasoning, or the style while leaving length and termination unchanged. The paper's own data show outputs did change in ways that matter. Finished accuracy goes 54.8->51.0 (Table 11). Matched finished accuracy falls 3.8 and 4.2 points with intervals excluding zero at seed 0. All-agree shares fall (14.6->12.0%). The paper reads the decline as a 'possible small decline', which implies the model changed. Either the 1e-5 declines are real, and then the adapter changed the outputs, or the outputs did not change, and then the declines are noise. The paper uses both readings in different places. The supporting evidence that 'the adapter therefore learns' (training loss 0.72->0.38) is also weak for this purpose: §3.4 says loss is computed over the whole chat sequence including the fixed prompt, so part of that drop may just be fitting the repeated template. To support the claim, a direct output-level measure is needed, for example \boxed/$ style shares by round at 1e-5 (as reported for the higher rates), per-problem added/lost churn compared with a resampling-of-base baseline, or token-level divergence between round-0 and round-4 generations. Otherwise 'little change' should be stated as an inference from length and cap-hit only.

title: 'Little change is a property of rate and steps together' is concluded from a comparison confounded by dataset
quote: is therefore a property of rate and steps together, not of the rate alone. A flat
explanation: Appendix E concludes that 'little change' depends on steps as well as rate, because Run C, at the same rate with about twice the steps (951 vs 436), does change its outputs. Run C is also the only GSM8K run. It differs from Run A in dataset, in base accuracy (66.7% vs 32%), and in cap-hit regime (3.5% vs 41–48%). The same appendix and §4.2 explicitly decline to attribute Run C's decline to the dataset alone, for exactly this reason. Attributing Run C's larger output change to steps is the mirror-image inference and needs the same hedge. Run C's time course also does not fit a per-round dose effect well: 9.3 of its 12.7 pass@1 points are lost in the final round, while the per-round dose is roughly constant or shrinking. App D then cites this inference ('Run C ... is the one 10^-5 run that declines clearly') as support for the Design P dose reading, so the conclusion rests on a single confounded comparison. It should be stated as one possible reading, not as a finding.

title: The 'dose explains level, not acceleration' argument is a false dichotomy, and dose does not even explain the level at round 1
quote: Dose also explains at most the level of the decline, not its time course: with a
explanation: The arithmetic checks out: the two largest pass@1 drops (-12.1 = 44.5->32.4 and -13.8 = 32.4->18.6) come from models trained on the pools of 3,395 and 2,638 examples. The inference drawn from it does not hold. (a) Dose and compounding through data interact rather than compete. Under restart-from-base, a larger per-round dose makes each round's model imitate its pool more strongly, so whatever drift is in the pool passes into the next generation faster. A high dose can therefore produce acceleration even while pool sizes shrink, so 'dose explains at most the level' does not follow. (b) The level is not explained by dose either. The round-1 model received the largest dose (3,962 examples, about 4.5x Run A) yet fell only 3.8 points (50.0->46.2), about the same as Design I Run A's round-1 drop of 2.7–5.3 points at 1x dose. On the dose reading the early level should differ most, and it does not. Together these suggest the collapse emerges over rounds, which fits a data-borne compounding mechanism amplified by dose more than either alone. The paper reaches a similar view ('something carried through the data ... fits this acceleration better'), but its stated reason splits the two mechanisms. The 1.5B pool shrinks by 60% (3,962->1,566) while the 0.5B pool shrinks only 16% (2,533->2,123); this is a further signal of compounding that could be used and is not discussed.

title: The 0.5B Design P run is the natural within-design control but is underused and has no uncertainty attached
quote: declines only a little, though it is a different model. Pooling or scoring may also
explanation: The 0.5B and 1.5B Design P runs share both structural features the paper lists as alternative explanations: pooled training on one adapter, and scoring on the selection set. The 0.5B run also has a large dose (2,533 examples, about 2.9x Run A, not far from the 1.5B's 4.5x). It shows only a mild, roughly linear decline (pass@1 -3.7, pass@8 -5.6) and little pool contraction. This is the strongest evidence in the paper that pooling and selection scoring are not sufficient on their own to produce the collapse. Yet App D closes with 'Pooling or scoring may also have contributed' without confronting it, and dismisses the 0.5B comparison only with 'it is a different model'. Several things are missing for 0.5B that are given for 1.5B: a per-dataset split (Table 9), style counts, a per-round pool trajectory (only the endpoints 2,533 to 2,123), and any interval on its decline. The main text calls the decline 'small' with no interval, even though the paper insists elsewhere on bootstrap intervals and patterns across runs. Either analyse the 0.5B run as the partial control it is, which narrows the candidate causes to model-by-dose interaction or compounding, or state clearly that it was not analysed and why.

title: Answer-diversity measures: stated scope contradicted by reported values, and the handling of cap-hit (no-answer) generations is unspecified
quote: (0.542 →0.554 for Run A, seed 0; 0.528 →0.543 for Run B, seed 1) but rises
explanation: App F says diversity was measured 'for Design P's 1.5B run and the 10^-5 Design I runs at seed 0'. The distinct-answer fraction is then reported for 'Run B, seed 1', which lies outside that scope. Either the scope or the label is wrong, and A and B are compared at different seeds and different partitions. More substantively, 41–48% of MATH-500 generations hit the token cap and mostly have no extractable answer, and in Design P \boxed usage halves. Neither the all-agree measure nor the distinct-answer measure says how a missing or unextractable answer is counted: as its own 'answer', as distinct each time, or excluded. That choice can by itself drive the reported movements, for example Design P's distinct fraction rising 0.443->0.712 and all-agree falling 24.8->1.7% as formatting drifts. The paper notes the link to cap-hits but gives no rule. Mixing selection and exam problems in Design I also mixes problems the model trained on with held-out ones. The paper draws no conclusion from these measures, which is appropriate, but the definitions need to be given for the numbers to be interpretable or reproducible.

title: Table 2's round-3 pass@8 corresponds to the default preset, contradicting 'the two presets gave identical pooled values'
quote: identical pooled values; a later per-dataset recomputation differs by one prob-
explanation: App D says Table 2 was computed during the run, 'where the two verifier presets gave identical pooled values'. Table 9's caption says that after recomputation the pooled round-3 pass@8 is 63.5% under the reward preset (the one used for selection, and per §3.4 the definition of 'correct') and 63.6% under the default preset. 63.6% is the value in Table 2. Recomputing from Table 9's per-dataset reward values gives (82.2+44.8)/2 = 63.5. So Table 2's R3 pass@8 matches the default preset rather than the reward preset. This is a one-problem difference with no effect on conclusions, but the 'identical' statement and the convention that 'correct' means the reward preset are not exactly true for Table 2. The caption could say which preset Table 2 uses. All other Table 2 entries reproduce exactly as averages of Table 9's two datasets, and all Table 2, 3 and 9 deltas recompute correctly.

title: 'Mostly real' argument for the train-on-gold decline is not bounded by the checks offered
quote: fall of about 19 points, and finished accuracy falls to 12–15%, so we think the fall
explanation: The concern is that the gold-trained model shifts strongly in format ($-spans 5%→98%, \boxed 52%→86%), and the same verifier grades the result. The paper offers three supports. (i) An exact-string match on boxed answers recovers 14/600 and 11/600 (≈2.3 and 1.8 points; checked). This is a lower bound, and the paper says so. (ii) The gold-storage re-score fixes a different defect, which the paper also concedes. (iii) Finished accuracy falls to 12–15% (Table 11: 14.7, 12.5). But (iii) is not independent evidence: finished accuracy is graded by the same verifier, so if the new style is misparsed it is misparsed in finished generations too. Nothing bounds the error from above. The ≈14% of round-2 generations with no \boxed are where math-verify falls back to the last LaTeX/$ span, and in a $-heavy reference style that span is often not the final answer. Those generations alone could account for up to ~14 points, and with the 2-point lower bound that is ~16 of the ~19-point fall. Equivalent-but-not-string-equal boxed answers are also uncounted. 'Even several times the first bound' is an arbitrary multiplier, not a bound. The conclusion may well be right, but a hand audit of a small random sample (e.g. 50 rejected round-2 generations per seed) is needed to support 'mostly real'. Otherwise the claim should be weakened to 'the share of verifier error is unmeasured; at least ~2 points of it is recoverable'.

title: No-filter control confounds more than dose (62% truncated training data), and learning-rate dependence is used as evidence that step count matters
quote: matter (the rate dependence above is suggestive), dose and data differ at once
explanation: The no-filter vs Run A deltas check out from Table 6 (pass@1 +4.0/−4.7, pass@4 −2.0/−5.3; sample-acc +0.2/−5.5 from Table 5's round-0 values). Two problems remain. (a) The paper names only optimizer steps (700 vs 220/196, 3.2–3.6×) as the confound. Table 11 shows a second, mechanistically relevant one: 62.4% of the no-filter round-0 pool is longer than the 512-token training limit, against 24.5% for Run A. The no-filter model is thus trained mostly on examples with no final answer and no EOS, the very mechanism §H tests with the 1,024-limit arm. A 2.5× higher share of unterminated training data, plus unfiltered wrong answers, plus 3–4× the steps, makes the comparison uninterpretable as an effect of the filter. That it nonetheless barely differs from Run A at seed 1 (cap-hit +2.3 vs +3.0) is itself informative about the truncation hypothesis and deserves mention. (b) The justification 'since dose may matter (the rate dependence above is suggestive)' conflates learning rate with number of optimizer steps. The rate sweep varies step size at a fixed step count, so even a firm rate dependence would not show that step count matters. Recommend listing truncation share as a confound and dropping or rephrasing the rate→dose inference.

title: Attribution between 'less accurate' and 'not finishing' rests on post-treatment conditioning and an untested counterfactual
quote: round-0 samples (6–21 problems, 34–37 in the gold runs), which, being mostly
explanation: The decomposition is arithmetically sound. I checked that the three parts sum to Δacc in every Table 7 row within rounding, and reproduced A seed 1 from Table 11 (s̄=0.553, Δf=−11.0 → −6.1; implied c=7.0%→4.7% → cap-acc −1.0; Δs=−3.0 × (f̄−c̄)=42.7 → −1.3). The interpretation is less secure, for three related reasons. (1) The matched metric conditions on finishing, an outcome of training. It drops the 22–45 problems (15–30% of the exam) where every last-round sample hits the cap, i.e. the problems most affected by non-termination. Within a problem, it also compares the round-0 finished samples with a different, selected subset at the last round, since when more samples run long, the ones that still finish are not a random draw. Matching on problem does not remove that within-problem selection. (2) The fallback baseline (all-sample round-0 accuracy for 6–21 problems, 34–37 for gold) is mostly cap-hit accuracy (4–7%). This biases the baseline down and so understates the matched decline. The paper notes the bias but not its direction for the headline '5–11 points'. In the gold runs a quarter of the problems use the fallback, so −25.6/−25.9 mixes two baselines. (3) The cap-share part Δs(f̄−c̄) values every generation that stops finishing at the average finished accuracy f̄. That assumes newly unfinished generations would have been as accurate as typical finished ones, but drift-prone generations are plausibly harder or already going wrong, which would make the termination share an overstatement. Conversely, the unmatched f in the finished part contains composition shifts. The 'Fin. share' percentages therefore depend on these assumptions as much as on the data. The text is careful ('descriptive'), but the abstract's 'mostly via less accurate finished solutions, partly via more cap-hits' framing should be stated as dependent on this counterfactual, and the direction of the fallback bias should be stated.

title: The 1,536-token re-score points to non-termination at seed 1, contrary to 'picture unchanged'
quote: cap leave the picture unchanged, within the noise of single runs (Appendix H).
explanation: At 512 tokens, the seed-1 anatomy says finished accuracy carries most of the decline (finished part 73–89% for A, replicate and 1024-limit; cap-share 12–30%). Table 12 at 1,536 tokens tells a different story for the same seed-1 adapters. Proxy 'Acc. finished' is nearly identical across rows (untrained 44.1, replicate 43.3, 1024-limit 41.3, 2e-4 40.8), while the 'Degenerate' share is 2.5% vs 23–33%. The arithmetic shows that the deficit is almost entirely the degenerate share. With degenerate generations scored ≈0, sample acc ≈ (1−deg)×acc_fin: untrained 0.975×44.1=43.0 (reported 43.2); replicate 0.77×43.3=33.3 (34.2); 1024-limit 0.673×41.3=27.8 (29.5). The −9.0 replicate deficit is thus ≈0.205×43 ≈ 8.8 points of non-termination and <1 point of finished accuracy. The proxy undercounts cap-hits, which contaminates 'Acc. finished' with low-accuracy unfinished text more for the adapters, so their true finished accuracy is if anything closer to the untrained model's. The appendix does say the re-score 'points to non-termination', but §4.5 summarises it as leaving the picture unchanged. With a larger budget the seed-1 adapters look like models that fail to stop, not models whose finished solutions are 5–9 points worse. That conflicts with the 512-token seed-1 split and with the abstract's emphasis on less accurate finished solutions. A second caveat: the untrained 512-token re-score (36.3%) is 2.6 points above the run's own round 0 (33.7%), inflating all deficits. For example, the 2×10⁻⁴ deficit is −7.8 here against −3.5 in Table 5. The §4.5 sentence should be revised, and the anatomy claim qualified by cap length.

title: 'Three rounds' and per-round step counts include a round-2 pool that trains no evaluated model
quote: 175, against 220, 196 and 163 for Run A at seed 1 (and 212, 193, 175 at seed 2).
explanation: Rounds are R0 (untrained), R1 (adapter on the R0 pool) and R2 (adapter on the R1 pool), so 'three rounds' at the higher rates means only two trained adapters, and each restarts from base. Yet the dose comparison lists three per-round step counts (220, 196, 163 = 440/2, 391/2, 326/2), and Tables 6/10 report a round-2 kept pool (326/350). The round-2 pool can only train an R3 adapter, which is never evaluated. Either a third adapter was trained and not reported, or the 163/175 figures are not optimizer steps behind any reported model. The steps relevant to the comparison are 220 and 196 (seed 1), giving 3.2–3.6× for no-filter and 0.8–0.9× for gold. These are consistent with '3–4×' and 'about the same', so the conclusion survives, but the listing invites the misreading that R2 reflects three rounds of training. Because of restart-from-base, the R2 model is one 196-step adapter trained on R1 outputs, not cumulative training. That should be stated wherever 'three rounds' or 'dose' is discussed (e.g. 'three evaluation points, two self-training iterations').

title: FN audit: the 'wrong-token extraction' diagnosis is probably confounded with the gold-storage defect, and the 7.8% has a restricted denominator and no interval
quote: the false-negative rate is 7.8% (10 of 128) on MATH-500
explanation: §3.2 says 'most failures are wrong-token extraction from a long solution'. The basis for the label is that 8 of 10 cases are 'accepted when only the boxed answer is' verified. Appendix B says most of these 8 are compound answers (3\sqrt{13}, 6−5i, 11\sqrt{2}, ...) and overlap with the bare-gold class. This raises a confound the paper does not rule out. If the extracted answer is passed without its box delimiter, it may be parsed exactly as the bare gold is (to its first number), and then match by accident. On that reading, the 'boxed-only accepted' test would show the gold-storage defect, not a long-solution extraction failure. The paper hedges that 'the two labels describe where the failure shows', but the main text still states the extraction diagnosis, and it presents the gold-storage defect as a separate post hoc discovery the audit apparently already saw. Also: the denominator keeps only answers the authors' normaliser recognises as correct (128 of 176). Compound answers are where both the normaliser and math-verify are weakest, so FN on exactly the problematic class is probably understated. The audit uses Qwen2.5-7B solutions, not the loop's outputs. And a Wilson interval is given for GSM8K 0/200 but not for MATH-500 10/128, which is roughly [4.3%, 13.8%]. The authors should state exactly what string was passed in the 'boxed-only' check, give the interval, and reconcile 7.8% with the loop's 15.5–18.4%, most of the gap probably being the unparseable-gold overlap.

title: Unparseable golds 'cancel within a partition' only for level offsets in differences, not for relative effects, conditional metrics or cross-partition comparisons
quote: which lowers absolute pass rates but cancels
explanation: The 51 unparseable golds (11–18 per exam partition) add a constant zero in each round, so they cancel in a within-run difference of sample accuracy or pass rates. But: (1) they dilute every change by the share of dead problems, 7–12% depending on the partition. Comparisons of decline size across seeds/partitions (e.g. 'the decline may grow with the rate on one seed', seed 1 vs seed 2) therefore carry partition-dependent dilution, and level comparisons across partitions carry offsets up to ~5 points (18 vs 11 dead problems). (2) Conditional and ratio measures do not cancel: matched finished accuracy, the finished/cap-share decomposition and the 'Fin. share' of Table 7, and r_t all include these problems. Their generations count as finished-but-wrong or cap-hit, so a change in termination on these problems moves 'finished accuracy' even though their correctness cannot change. (3) Under V′ they become scorable (46/51), so the 'cancellation' is exactly what makes original and re-scored changes differ (see the factor issue). The paper should state the number of dead problems per partition, and preferably report the main metrics with these problems excluded.

title: Training limit of 512 tokens including the prompt, with a 512-new-token generation cap, means accepted examples are trained without their answer or EOS
quote: with a training sequence limit of 512 tokens
explanation:
Any kept solution can be up to 512 generated tokens, but the training sequence (prompt + solution) is cut at 512. With standard right-truncation, every kept solution longer than 512 − (prompt length) loses its ending: the final \boxed answer and the end-of-turn/EOS token. The summary reports 24–26% of the pool truncated. Two consequences matter for the paper's claims. (a) For a quarter of the pool, the verifier filter does not actually decide what is trained on: the trained text no longer contains the verified answer, so these are not 'kept correct solutions' in the GVT sense. (b) Training on sequences that stop mid-solution without EOS directly teaches non-termination. That is a plausible mechanism for the cap-hit increases at 5e-4 that §4.5 decomposes, and a design-induced cause of decline rather than a property of self-training. The paper does test this partly (one 1024-limit run and one retrain without truncated examples, both at seed 1, reported 'within the noise of single runs'). But the main configuration has the flaw, no rationale is given for setting the limit equal to the generation cap, and the truncation side is not stated. It also matters that the 1024-limit run (−5.7) is closer to the same-configuration replicate (−5.2) than to the original (−8.3). The method should state truncation side and EOS handling, give the truncation rate per run, and either fix the limit or treat it as a named confound in the conclusions about decline.

Related: Loss over the prompt is an unjustified, unablated design choice that interacts with duplicate problems and with the token budget — Computing loss on the prompt departs from standard rejection-sampling SFT (completion-only loss), and no reason is given. In this setup a problem can contribute up to k accepted solutions, so its statement and the fixed instruction are trained up to k times per round. At 5e-4 this adds a strong gradient signal unrelated to solving and invites memorising the problem text. It also uses part of the 512-token training budget, which worsens truncation of the solution. Because the paper attributes declines at high learning rates to self-training dynamics (less accurate finished solutions, more cap-hits), a training-objective choice that could itself cause degradation should be justified or ablated, or at least listed among the confounds. The paper should also state the per-round count of duplicate problems and whether samples were deduplicated.

title: Reproducibility gaps: what a 'seed' controls, where replicate nondeterminism comes from, shared round-0 generations, and the inference setup
quote: A “seed” sets the exam partition, the selection set and the training
explanation: A seed is said to fix the partition, the selection set and the training randomness. Yet a 'same-configuration' replicate (Run A, 5e-4, seed 1) ends 3.2 points away, and Runs A and B at seed 2 have identical round-0 pools (424) but end 7.3 points apart in pass@1. If training and sampling were fully seeded, identical pools would give identical round-1 adapters. So something is not controlled (fp16 GPU nondeterminism, unseeded or batch-dependent sampling, data-loader order). The paper never says what, although these replicate gaps are used to calibrate training-seed variance. Also unstated: whether round-0 generations are produced once and shared across runs with the same seed (Tables 4 and 6 show identical R0 values 33.3/50.0/33.7 across three rates, which suggests they are); the generation engine and batching/padding (HF generate vs vLLM, fp16); whether the chat template's default system prompt is included; whether multiple accepted samples of the same problem are deduplicated; truncation side; and how cap-hit was recorded (re-tokenising to ≥508 rather than using the generation's finish reason is an approximation and should be justified). These details decide whether the runs can be reproduced, and they bear directly on the paper's noise arguments.
