title: All headline numbers are graded by a verifier known to reject ~1/6 of correct answers; 'the loop trained with it' does not justify using it as the evaluation measure
quote: “Correct” always means accepted by the verifier (preset reward), the
explanation: The same verifier V selects training data and grades the held-out exam. The paper then finds that V rejects 15.5–18.4% of V′-accepted generations, yet keeps V in every table, 'since that is the verifier the loop trained with'. That is a reason to use V for selection, not for measuring mathematical ability, which is the research question. For the 'no gain' claim, grading with V is partly conservative: adaptation to V would raise V-scores, so an absence of V-gains is informative. But for magnitudes (declines, finished-accuracy losses, the decomposition, the 2.2 bound), the better-calibrated grader should be primary, or both should be shown side by side. Re-scoring is cheap (saved generations, CPU-only), and only five runs were re-scored, so the conclusions that all other declines 'would also survive a re-score' rest on extrapolation from three. Re-scoring all runs with V′, plus an independent check (e.g. the scripted normaliser), would remove most of the factor/extrapolation issues above.

title: The illustrative example of the gold-storage defect is written backwards
quote: so a correct boxed prediction can fail against a bare gold (e.g. \frac43
explanation: The sentence describes a boxed prediction failing against a bare gold, but the example reads '\frac43 against \boxed{\frac{4}{3}}', which shows a bare form against a boxed one, apparently the other way round. It is also not clear which of \frac43 / \frac{4}{3} is the stored gold. Appendix B's mechanism ('the bare gold is parsed to its first number') makes this matter: for gold '\frac43' the first number would be 4, so a correct 4/3 would fail and a wrong '4' would pass. That is the false-positive channel raised in a separate comment. A precise example (stored gold string, prediction string, what each side parses to) would remove the ambiguity.

title: Abstract states post hoc results without the post hoc label the body attaches to them
quote: gains above 2.2 points, a loose bound that omits training-seed variance.
explanation: §3.4 says that claims resting on sample accuracy, 'including the 2.2-point bound, are therefore post hoc in the choice of measure'. §4.5 calls the finished-accuracy analysis 'post hoc and descriptive', and App H says the matched metric 'conditions on an outcome of training and is descriptive, not a causal effect'. The abstract qualifies the 2.2-point bound only for seed variance, not for the post hoc choice of measure or the lack of an equivalence margin. It also gives 'finished solutions become 5–11 points less accurate' as a plain headline finding, with no mention that it comes from a post hoc, post-treatment-conditioned metric. That metric drops 22–45 problems per run and uses a baseline that App H admits is biased for 6–21 problems. The abstract does label the r_t test 'post hoc', so the labelling is inconsistent. The paper applies its own standard of marking post hoc analyses in the body but relaxes it exactly where readers look first.

title: 'Five of six runs' counts near-replicates and runs that share a baseline as independent evidence
quote: vals excluding zero in five of six runs, while the cap-hit share rises 2–14 points.
explanation: The six 5×10^-4 MATH-500 runs (A, B, no-filter at seeds 1 and 2) come from only two exam partitions. Within a seed, all three share the same round-0 generations, so the matched baseline is shared, and A and B share almost all of their pool. §4.4 says correctly that 'same-seed A and B are closer to two replicates than four', and App E/I.1 make the same point for A and B at seed 0 at 10^-5. §4.5 and I.1 still report 'five of six' as if it were six independent confirmations; the same goes for the cap-hit statement 'in all three seed-2 runs'. Since seed sets the partition, these really amount to two partition-level observations with correlated intervals. Reporting them as 'both partitions' (with the per-seed pattern) would be consistent with the paper's own replicate accounting.

title: The cap-share split by seed is called 'qualitative' and possibly partition noise in App H, but is said to move the reading in §5.3
quote: the split moves the reading: at 5 × 10−4 the cap share accounts for 12–30% of
explanation: App H says the finished-accuracy shares 'have wide intervals' (e.g. 59% [−11, 114], 73% [43, 108]), that they split by seed, that 'this may be partition variation', and that 'What the table supports is qualitative'. §5.3(ii), the proposed audit protocol, and I.1 nonetheless present 12–30% versus 52–72% as a substantive finding that 'moves the reading'. These are ratios of two noisy differences, which are unstable when the total change is small (A, seed 2: −4.7), and the seed-1 and seed-2 intervals overlap. The ranges are point estimates over near-replicate runs (see the five-of-six comment). §5.3 should carry the App H caveat, or report the cap-share part in points with intervals rather than as a percentage of the decline.

title: The 'about four of 76 by chance' heuristic is misapplied and used one-sidedly
quote: at the 95% level about four of the 76 would exclude zero by chance if nothing
explanation: The expected count of 76×0.05 ≈ 4 assumes the global null holds for all 76 intervals. Many are plainly non-null: train-on-gold (−18 to −26), Run C (−12 to −22), and most 5×10^-4 rows. The number of intervals for which 'nothing changed' is plausible is much smaller, so the expected count of false exclusions among them is lower, about 1–2 if roughly 30 are near-null. The count also includes the post hoc matched column, which uses a different re-scoring and 2,000 resamples. App E uses the heuristic to discount the 10^-5 seed-0 declines, but the multiplicity argument is not turned on the no-gain conclusion. There, the relevant issue is that the reported bound is the maximum of about 13 upper ends, so its joint coverage is below nominal. A family-wise or false-discovery-rate adjustment over a defined family (e.g. the 13 self-training Δsample-acc intervals), or a pooled analysis, would apply the multiplicity standard in both directions.

title: 'Fixed in advance' covers the measures only: the design itself (rates, k, rounds, controls) was adaptive, and no registration record is given
quote: Because 10−5 changed the MATH-500 outputs little, we reran Run A at 10−4
explanation: The introduction says four measures and a reading rule were 'fixed in advance', which suggests pre-registration. No registration or timestamped protocol is cited. The learning-rate grid, the switch to k=4 and three rounds, the controls and the replicate were all chosen after seeing the 10^-5 results, and the primary measure, the cap-hit definition, the matched metric, the decomposition and the r_t test were all added afterwards. The paper is admirably open about most of these individually. Still, a headline such as 'no gain at four learning rates' comes from a sequence of data-dependent design choices, and Δpass@k mixes k=8 (10^-5) with k=4 (other rates). One sentence stating that only pass@1, pass@k, \boxed share and transitions plus the reading rule were pre-set, and that the rest of the design was adaptive, would prevent readers from crediting the study with more pre-specification than it had.
